messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Religious Educator
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Linh was thirty-two years old when her village was overrun. She had been walking home from the market with a basket of vegetables when the first shells hit the rice paddies. The smell of wet earth and smoke flooded her nostrils—a smell she would later recognize anywhere, a smell that could stop her breath. She ran toward her house, but the thatch was already burning. She saw a soldier grab her neighbor by the arm and pull her into the flames. Linh’s own body froze. She could not move. She could not scream. The heat pressed against her skin, and then—nothing. She has no memory of how she escaped. Only that she woke up in a ditch, covered in mud and ash, with the taste of blood on her lips. The next three days are a gray smear. She knows from others that she walked to a refugee camp, but she does not feel that memory as hers. It feels like a story about someone else. What she does feel, with a vividness that ordinary memories cannot match, is the moment she saw the soldier’s hand close around her neighbor’s arm. That image is more real to her than her own wedding day.

For the next forty-eight years, Linh built a quiet life in the United States as a religious educator at a small Buddhist temple. She taught dharma classes to children and led meditation groups. She married a kind man who understood her silences. But the past never really left her. It lived in her body. When a student would touch her shoulder without warning, she would flinch so violently that the child would pull back in alarm. She began to insist that no one approach her from behind. At the temple’s annual Bon Odori festival, the sight of the bonfire would send her heart racing and her hands trembling; she would excuse herself to the kitchen until it was extinguished. She came to believe that her own body had betrayed her—that the panic she felt was proof she was broken. Worse, she was certain that the bombing had happened because of something wrong in her. She had not been a good enough person. She had not prayed enough. She felt a deep, permanent humiliation, as though everyone could see that she was the sort of person whom disaster found.

The intrusive memories came without warning, but she learned to push them away. She kept her mind occupied every waking hour—planning lessons, reciting sutras, counting the seconds in a breath. She checked the locks on her doors and windows three times before bed, then again in the middle of the night. She had no interest in making new friends. Old acquaintances from the temple would invite her to lunch, and she would decline with a polite excuse. She told herself she was simply too tired, but the truth was that she could not bear the thought of being vulnerable with another person. The only people she trusted were her husband and one childhood friend who had also fled the war. Even with her husband, she never spoke of the ditch or the fire or the soldier’s hand.

The cracks finally widened a year ago, when her temple hosted a commemorative ceremony for wartime refugees. A speaker described a burning village, and the phrase “smell of wet earth” launched a flashback so intense that Linh could not breathe. She wept in the parking lot for twenty minutes and then drove home in silence. Her husband, who had always respected her privacy, gently told her that he could not watch her suffer anymore. That night, she admitted to herself that she had been living in a cage of her own making. The memory gaps haunted her—she wanted to fill them, but she was terrified of what she might find. The alien quality of the memory made her feel like a fraud: how could she be so afraid of something that did not even feel like hers? She had built a life of teaching and compassion, but she could not extend that compassion to her own younger self.

At eighty, she has finally agreed to see a therapist. Her hope is modest: she wants to stop checking the locks every night. She wants to sit by a bonfire without feeling that she is about to die. But what she fears most is that she will be asked to remember what happened in those missing days, and that the answer will confirm everything she has always believed about herself.
